doc.title: Bill Crow interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: Buzzy's lesson on swing and Gus Johnson's drumming
summary: Buzzy Bridgeford taught him what swinging means; he praises Gus Johnson's time and later hired him for Mulligan's quartet.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: What was it about that rhythm section that made it so identifiable?

Well by that time of course I had memorized the Basie records. That was one of the things Buzzy did for me when I first met him in Seattle, was he said, “You don’t know about the Count Basie band?” He got out all the, especially the old Deccas with Lester on them, and played me all of those things. And he listened to me play drums a couple of times when I was at jam sessions and things, and he liked the way I played well enough to send me in to sub for him, because he knew I didn’t play as well as he did and I couldn’t take his job away. But he sat me down one day in his room and he said, “What do you think about when you play the drums?” You know, I said, “Well I think about putting the beats in the right place and not speeding up and not slowing down, and that seemed to be the big issue with the rest of the band.” He said, “Well yeah but what about swinging?” I said, “I don’t really know what that means, I’ve heard that term but I don’t really know what that means.” And I couldn’t have asked a better guy, because he was the one person I’ve ever met in my life that was able to describe it. He put on some really swinging records. I remember there was a V disc he had of Duke playing “Jumpin’ Punkins” that was a much better take than the one they released on Victor, and three or four others, like “Poundcake” from the Basie band and “Avenue C” and some of those things. And he got up and danced out the swing and showed me, “Now look what the drummer’s doing here.” You know, say “Look what happens, look what the band did there, look what this arrangement causes to happen, look what the soloist did there.” All © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

in rhythmic terms, and I just, it was like the scales fell from my eyes, I saw immediately what he was talking about. And from then on I had some kind of an ideal, rhythmically, to shoot for. So that was when I got to hear this version of the Basie band, I thought Gus Johnson was ideal, because he was doing the same kind of thing in the rhythm section. Gus had an interesting style of playing his cymbal beat was kind of up on the top of the beat. And it wasn’t a loose, you know, the way the time is divided in swing, each of the four beats has a kind of a triplet division rather than rock divides it by two, jazz divides it by three. And that quality that Jo Jones had kind of established of [scats] it’s like a loose pattern that he always played that you heard behind everything, Gus’ was a little more [scats]. It was, the triplet was pushed up a little farther. But when he would play a figure around the drums, it would be laid back. It would almost be behind the beat. And the combination of those two, it kept the time up where it belonged, so he was right on Freddie Green’s time, and at the same time he encouraged that loose phrasing that the band had. I thought he was the ideal drummer. I was very disappointed with they replaced him with Sonny Payne, although I could see why they did it. Sonny was a showman. But I didn’t think that, to sacrifice the heartbeat of that band to a showman was the right move. Commercially I guess it was a very good move. Basie took his manager’s advice about it. But I tell you, I liked Gus so much that years later when neither Mel Lewis or Dave Bailey were available for a Gerry Mulligan quartet job, and Gerry asked us for recommendations, I said I know Gus Johnson’s not doing anything right now, and I talked them into hiring him and he stayed with us for about year. I thought he was a wonderful addition to that group.
